sections.body:
A passport is not a personal possession. It is a document issued by your own government to a named holder, and it proves two things at once: who you are, and that your country allows you to leave it. That second half is why a passport cannot simply be replaced by a private company or by a photocopy.

The moment a passport goes missing, the document stays valid in the eyes of the issuing country until it is formally reported as lost. That is the central fact of this whole situation, and it works both ways: the passport cannot be used by anybody else, and you cannot be left without a way home, because your government has a duty to return you.

So a lost passport is a **bureaucratic problem**, and the whole game is doing the right thing in the right order. The correct order is almost always the same: report the loss to the police where it happened, report it to your own embassy or consulate, then apply for a replacement passport or an **emergency travel document**.

There are two kinds of replacement. A **new passport** is the full document, and it can take days or weeks because it is made abroad. An **emergency travel document** or **emergency passport** is a short-validity document for a single journey home, and it can often be issued the same day or the next morning. Which one you can get depends on your nationality, on the country you are in, and on how far you are from home.

One more distinction matters. **Lost** means you cannot find it. **Stolen** means somebody took it. **Mislaid** means it is probably still where you left it. The words describe different situations to a police officer and to an insurance company, and they lead to different questions, so choose the true one rather than the most dramatic one.

A lost passport also stops other things, and it is worth knowing what they are before you start. You cannot normally rent a car, buy a ticket in your own name, open a bank account, or board a domestic flight. You may not be able to prove your age for a bar or a pension. Each of these has a workaround for some people and no workaround for others, and the workaround usually depends on the same thing: evidence of identity.

That is why the question at the heart of every lost-passport case is simple. What do you still have that proves who you are? A national identity card, a driver's licence, a copy of the passport, a photograph of the passport page, a colleague who can vouch for you, an entry stamp from the country you arrived in. The answer decides how fast you get home.
examples: I have lost my passport and I need to report it.
I need an emergency travel document to get home.
sections.heading: What a lost passport actually is, and what happens next

sections.body:
This is the sequence that works. Doing it out of order means a second trip to the police station, and in a foreign country a second trip is expensive and tiring.

Retrace your steps, for fifteen minutes. Check the hotel safe, the taxi, the coat pocket, the café table, the bag that went through security. A large share of lost passports are found, and a found passport ends the whole problem.

If it is genuinely gone, secure the rest of your documents. Everything else you are carrying, especially your bank cards, your other identity documents and your phone, should be kept together and out of sight. If you suspect theft, change your bank passwords first, because a stolen passport plus a stolen card is a much larger problem.

Go to the local police. A loss report is usually a requirement for the embassy, and many embassies will not accept an application without it. Take the loss report, with its reference number, to the embassy.

Contact your embassy or consulate. Many missions have an emergency number, and in a crisis they will tell you to come to a specific office and at a specific hour. Call before you travel to the address, because consular services are often in a different building from the main embassy, and sometimes only open on certain days.

Ask precisely for what you need. Say clearly that you want to travel home, say when you need to leave, and ask what they issue for that. Do not leave the decision to the officer: explain the flight, the date and the deadline.

Keep every receipt and every reference number. The loss report number, the embassy application number, the receipt for the fee, and the courier tracking number. These are what turn an impossible situation into a series of small, solvable steps.
examples: I need to report a lost passport and I would like a copy of the report.
Which office should I come to, and what time does it open?
I have a flight on Friday. What document can I get by then?
sections.heading: The first hour, in the right order
steps: Retrace your steps for fifteen minutes and check the hotel safe and your bags.
Gather and secure your remaining documents, cards and phone.
Report the loss at the local police and get a written report.
Call your embassy or consulate and ask where and when to come.
Bring the police report, your ID and any copies you hold.
Ask for the document that fits your travel date.
Keep every receipt and reference number in one place.

sections.body:
These are the words that appear on the forms and in the conversations, and knowing them makes the process much faster.

An **embassy** is the official diplomatic mission of your country in another country, and it issues your passport. A **consulate** is a smaller office, usually in a city other than the capital, doing the same work for a region. Some countries have neither in a place, and refer you to the nearest embassy in another country; that is normal, and it is why you should check the official website of your own foreign ministry rather than guess.

A **loss report** is the official record that a document has been lost. A **police report** or **report to the police** is the same thing made by the local police, and it is the one the embassy usually asks for, because only the local police can confirm what happened on local ground.

An **emergency travel document**, also called an **emergency passport** or a **temporary travel document**, is a one-way or short-validity document issued so you can return home. It is usually valid for one or two journeys and for a short period. It is not a substitute for a proper passport at the end of the trip: if you plan to keep travelling, you will need the real one too.

A **replacement passport** is the normal new document. **Consular assistance** or **consular services** is the general help an embassy gives to its own citizens, including a lost passport, a hospital admission, a death in the family, or a legal problem abroad.
examples: Do I need a police report for the consulate?
What does the emergency travel document allow me to do?
Can you tell me the reference number of my loss report?
sections.heading: The words you will need at the police station and the embassy

terms.example: The embassy gave me an emergency document the same morning.
terms.gloss: The official office of your country in another country. It issues your passport and provides consular help.

terms.example: There is no embassy here, only a consulate, and it opens at nine.
terms.gloss: A smaller embassy office in a city other than the capital, serving a region. It does the same passport work.

terms.example: The emergency travel document is valid for this flight and one return.
terms.gloss: A short-validity passport issued so you can return home, often same day. It normally allows one or two journeys.

terms.example: Here is my police report; the reference number is on the first page.
terms.gloss: The written record the local police make about a loss or theft. Most embassies require one before issuing any document.

terms.example: I have already filed the loss report for my passport.
terms.gloss: The official declaration that a document has been lost. It is what cancels the old document in the issuing country's records.

sections.body:
One honest fact first. Not every country has a mission of your country. Smaller states, and countries where the number of citizens travelling is low, often have neither an embassy nor a consulate. When that happens, three things are true.

You are normally covered by the mission in a nearby country, and sometimes by a mission much further away, depending on where you are on the map. This arrangement is called **consular jurisdiction**: one mission looks after a group of countries at once. The list is published on the website of your own foreign ministry, usually under consular services or consular districts.

That mission may be far away, and it may work only by appointment. So the first call is not always to the closest embassy. It is to the office that has jurisdiction over the place where you are standing, using the emergency number published on its own website.

Two practical consequences follow. First, distance changes the plan: a mission in another country may need a courier, may take several days, and may not issue a document at all if you are not a resident of its jurisdiction. Second, your documents and your money have to travel further too, which is why clear photocopies and a way to pay remotely matter so much.

And if you are not on land, the rules change again. A passport problem on a cruise ship is handled by the flag state of the ship and by the cruise line, not by a local police station. At an airport in transit, the airline's ground staff can usually open a file and start the process, because the airline is responsible for carrying you home.

So when you are unsure which rule applies, ask two questions, in this order: who has jurisdiction over this place, and who has jurisdiction over me. The answer to the first decides who you call. The answer to the second decides what you can actually get.
examples: Which mission covers this country? I could not find a consulate here.
Can that office issue me a document, or only forward my application?
I am on a cruise and my passport was stolen in port. Who do I report to?
sections.heading: When your country has no mission where you are

sections.body:
The police report feels like a formality, and for most people it is. It is not. It is the document that proves the passport is not in your hands any more, and in most countries the embassy will not issue a replacement without it.

Find the right station. For a loss in a hotel, the hotel's staff can usually tell you which station handles foreign nationals, and in some countries there is a special desk for passport losses at the main station. In a country where you are reporting a theft, the station may be the one for your area of the city rather than the one near the hotel.

Describe it in plain facts. Where and when you last had it, what you were doing, whether the bag was stolen or the item simply vanished, and whether you have any suspicion about where it might be. Do not invent details. An honest account of an honest accident is much easier to act on than an inconsistent story, and inconsistency is what turns a routine report into a long investigation.

Ask for a certificate, not just a note on a form. What you need is a document that states the passport details and that it was reported lost, ideally with a **reference number** and an official stamp. A vague slip with no numbers may be rejected by the embassy, and then you go back to the station. Check before you leave that the document contains: your full name as in the passport, your nationality, the passport number, the date and place of loss, and the date of the report.

Ask about the copy. In some countries the police will keep the passport details and give you a certified copy, which the embassy may accept in place of the original. In others they will not. Ask.

Keep it. Photograph it. Keep the report in a document folder, not loose in a bag, and take a clear photograph of every page. You will be asked for it more than once, and the second time you may not have it with you.
examples: I need a certificate that reports my passport as lost, with a reference number.
Last saw it yesterday evening in my hotel room.
Could I have a certified copy of this report for the embassy?
sections.heading: Reporting the loss to the police

sections.body:
An embassy is run like an office, and it will check the same things in the same order. Arriving with the right things turns a week into a morning.

Identity. Without your passport you must prove you are who you say you are. The usual evidence is a national identity card, a driver's licence, a previous passport, or a copy of the lost passport. A passport photograph from your old file, if your government issues one, is worth having.

Proof of the loss. The police report.

The application form. Download it from the embassy website before you go if you can, and fill it in as far as you can. Most embassies also have forms at the desk, but downloading saves an hour and lets you write slowly.

Photographs. Two passport photographs of yourself, taken recently, with a plain background. Many embassies sell photographs on site, so ask before you panic, but having your own removes one dependency.

Payment. The fee is usually modest and is payable in the local currency or by card, and some embassies do not accept foreign cards. Bring cash in small denominations. Fees are not refundable, so be sure of what you are applying for before you pay.

The old passport number. You should know it, and if you do not, the police report often contains it, since the officer will have copied it from your other documents or from a copy you showed them.

A written explanation of your situation. Two or three sentences on paper: where you are, when you need to travel, what happened, and how you will get home. This is what the officer will read if you are not in the room when they call you, and it prevents a long explanation in a second language.

At the desk, expect to fill a form, show documents, pay a fee, and be given an appointment or a collection time. Ask for everything in writing: the receipt, the application reference, and the date and place of collection.
examples: Here is my national identity card and two photographs.
I need to travel home on Friday. Which document should I apply for?
Can I have a receipt and the collection date in writing?
sections.heading: At the embassy: what to bring and what they will ask

terms.example: They put me in contact with consular assistance straight away.
terms.gloss: The general help your embassy gives to its own citizens abroad, including lost documents, medical emergencies and legal problems.

terms.example: The replacement passport will be ready in five working days.
terms.gloss: A new full passport issued after the old one is reported lost. It takes longer than an emergency document but works normally.

sections.body:
You may still need to describe your passport, and you should be able to recognise a genuine one. These are the features that matter.

A **biometric symbol**, the little rectangle with a circle and a line inside it, marks a document with an embedded chip. It usually sits under the photo on the cover. An **e-passport** is read electronically at the border, and it is worth knowing because some embassies can verify it from another source, which speeds everything up.

The **machine-readable zone** is the two lines of small print at the bottom of the photo page. It encodes your name, nationality, date of birth and passport number. It is the part that should be copied, never by hand but by a photocopy or a photo, when you make your set of copies.

The **visa pages** are the pages with stamps and visas in them. In a lost passport, the visas you held are gone with it, and this is a real cost: a valid visa in a lost passport is usually not enough to travel on, and some countries require a new visa issued into the replacement document.

The **nationality and passport number** on the identity page are the two facts you must be able to give. The **expiry date** matters too, because if the passport was close to expiry, your embassy will refuse the emergency-document route and insist on a full replacement.

And a **signature** at the bottom of the photo page: many travellers do not sign their passport, and some countries require it. A signature that does not match the one on your ticket can cause an unpleasant argument at the border.
examples: My passport is biometric, so the number is on the machine-readable page.
Is there a signature line at the bottom of the photo page?
What is the passport number and the expiry date?
sections.heading: The marks on a passport worth knowing

symbols.meaning: A rectangle with a circle and a line: the biometric chip symbol, meaning the passport is an electronic document.
Two lines of small print under the photo: the machine-readable zone, which encodes your name, nationality, date of birth and passport number.
The page marked VISA or VISAS: pages that carry the visas and stamps of countries you have visited.
The small box in the top corner of the pages: the page number of the document.

sections.body:
Waiting too long to report it. Every day you wait is a day your old passport could still be found and used. Report it the same day, even if you hope it turns up.

Failing to cancel it in the records. A loss report tells the issuing country to cancel the document. If you only tell the embassy and not the police, the cancellation may not be triggered, and you may be given a document while a valid passport is still open in the system.

Using a photocopy as a travel document. A photocopy of a passport is not a passport. Border officers in most countries will refuse it, and you will be at the desk with no remedy.

Leaving your new document somewhere and losing it again. Put it in an inner pocket, a money belt, or a hotel safe, and never carry it in a backpack on your back in a crowd.

Not checking the expiry date. If your passport has less than six months left, many countries will refuse entry on it, and the emergency-document route may be closed to you.

Forgetting the visa. A visa in a lost passport does not travel with you. If your route needs a visa, check whether you can get a new one into the replacement document, and how long that takes.

Leaving the receipts behind. The fee receipt and the collection slip are proof of what you applied for and when. Losing them means going back.
sections.heading: The mistakes that turn a lost passport into a lost trip

sections.body:
A replacement passport can take days. This is the period people find hardest, because you are a traveller without documents in a country that does not know you.

Stay in contact with the embassy. Ask how they will reach you: a phone number, an email, or a mobile phone number you keep switched on. Some embassies will send a courier to your hotel if you cannot travel to collect.

Your status while you wait. Being without a passport does not automatically make you illegal, but it can leave you with no right to work, no right to open a bank account, and no way to prove who you are to anyone. The embassy will usually tell you what status you have and for how long. Ask, in writing if you can.

Money. Get access to your own money before the problem starts, not after. The useful habits are a card that works abroad, a second card stored somewhere different from the first, and a small emergency fund in cash in a second currency. If your passport is gone, some banks will not talk to you without it, so ask your bank in advance what they need to restore access: an app, a photograph of the card, a branch visit with a photograph.

Accommodation. Most hotels will let you pay at the end of the stay with a card if you can show the passport, and some will not. Book with a booking reference and the name on your other ID, and keep the confirmation. Ask the embassy if there is any arrangement for travellers in this situation.

Travel insurance. Read the policy now. Most travel insurance covers the cost of an emergency travel document, and some cover the cost of the extra hotel nights, the transport home, or the loss of money. The insurer will want the police report, so this is a second reason to make that report properly. Claiming later is much harder than claiming promptly.
examples: I have no passport. Can I still check in with a photograph of my ID and the police report?
What is my legal status in this country until I get the document?
Can I claim the cost of the emergency passport from my insurance?
sections.heading: While you wait: staying legal, housed and able to pay

terms.example: My travel insurance covers the emergency document and two extra hotel nights.
terms.gloss: A policy that covers things like medical care, cancellation, lost documents and the cost of an emergency replacement passport.

sections.body:
Almost every lost passport is lost to one of a small number of ordinary causes, and each has a cheap fix.

Leaving it in a bag or a pocket. The fix is to keep the passport in one place only: a zipped compartment against the body, a neck pouch, or a hotel safe. Never in a jacket pocket, never loose in a rucksack, never in a café bag while you walk away.

A photocopy that does not exist. Make a set before you travel: a photocopy of the identity page, a photograph of it on your phone, a photograph of the back, and a second copy at home or in cloud storage. With those, replacing a passport takes days instead of weeks, because the embassy can verify you without the original. Keep them separately from the originals.

Not writing down the details. On a separate card, write your passport number, the issue and expiry dates, the issuing authority, and the phone number of your embassy or consulate in the country you are going to. If the passport is lost, you cannot look these up; if you can look them up, everything is faster.

Not telling your bank and your phone provider. Save your bank's international number and your mobile provider's number in your phone under your own name, and keep a copy at home. A frozen phone with no passport is a very bad afternoon.

Not separating the passport from the bag. Take it out of your hand luggage before you check the bag, and put it back afterwards. The single most common loss is putting a passport into a checked suitcase and then travelling without it.

And one habit worth starting today: check that you know where your passport is. Right now, before you travel, not at the airport.
examples: I keep a photocopy of my passport at home and a photo on my phone.
I write my passport number and the embassy number on a card in my wallet.
I take the passport out of my hand bag before checking it.
sections.heading: How to make sure it does not happen again

terms.example: I keep a copy of my passport at home and one in my email.
terms.gloss: A set of photocopies or photographs of your identity documents, kept apart from the originals, so they can be replaced quickly.

item.summary: Losing a passport is a bureaucratic problem, not a disaster, but only if you act in the right order. After reading this you can report the loss correctly, get the right documents from the right office, and travel home while you wait.
item.title: What to Do When You Lose Your Passport
